source.text: אֵיכָה֩ יָעִ֨יב בְּאַפּ֤וֹ׀אֲדֹנָי֙ אֶת־בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן הִשְׁלִ֤יךְ מִשָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ אֶ֔רֶץ תִּפְאֶ֖רֶת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְלֹא־זָכַ֥ר הֲדֹם־רַגְלָ֖יו בְּי֥וֹם אַפּֽוֹ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: How covers-with-a-cloud in his anger [the] Lord the daughter of Zion! He has thrown from heavens [to] earth [the] splendor of Israel, and not has he remembered [the] footstool of his feet in [the] day of his anger.

en.L: How the Lord in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger has covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud! \q He has thrown down from heaven to earth the splendor of Israel, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has not remembered the footstool of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet in the day of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger.
en.B: How the Lord in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger has covered Daughter Zion with a cloud! \q He has hurled the splendor of Israel down from heaven to earth; \q in the day of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave no thought to the footstool of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.
en.R: How the Lord has covered the people of Zion with the dark cloud of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger! \q He threw the beauty of Israel down from heaven to the ground. \q When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was angry, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not even remember {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} footstool, the temple.

decisions.choice: an alphabet poem: twenty-two verses, one for each letter
decisions.reason: Like chapters 1 and 4, this chapter is an acrostic: each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph here to taw in verse 22. Here the letter pe (verse 16) comes before ayin (verse 17), the reverse of the order in chapter 1; chapter 3 (verses 46-51) and chapter 4 (verses 16-17) do the same. Some early alphabet inscriptions found in Israel also put pe before ayin, so the poet may be following an older order of the letters. The verses keep the three-line lament rhythm described at 1:1.

decisions.choice: How ...!: a cry of grief and shock, and the book's Hebrew title
decisions.reason: The word ('ekhah) is an exclamation, not a question: the cry of a mourner over the dead (compare Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah 48:17), here over a fallen city. It opens chapters 1, 2 and 4, and it is the Hebrew name of the book.

decisions.choice: has covered with a cloud: has darkened her in his anger
decisions.reason: The verb is found only here. It is usually taken from the word for a cloud: God's anger settles over Zion like a dark cloud, where once his cloud of glory filled the temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). Others link it to a different root meaning "to treat with contempt" or "to disgrace".

decisions.choice: the footstool of his feet: the ark and the temple on Zion
decisions.reason: The ark of the covenant and the temple where it stood are called God's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:5; 132:7). "The splendor of Israel" is the same city and temple, the pride of the nation, flung down like a star falling from the sky (Isaiah 14:12).

decisions.choice: the poet speaks about Zion, and the Lord is the one acting
decisions.reason: Chapter 1 ended with Zion speaking (1:22). Here the poet's voice returns and describes Zion from outside, through verse 10. Almost every verb in verses 1-8 has the Lord as its subject: the enemy's work is described as his.

decisions.choice: the people of Zion ... his footstool, the temple
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people of Zion" for "daughter of Zion", as Isaiah does: the city is pictured as a daughter, and the picture stands for its people. It also names the temple, which the footstool stands for (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: How ...!
decisions.reason: As at 1:1, every level keeps "How" with an exclamation mark (m2).

source.text: בִּלַּ֨ע אֲדֹנָ֜י וְלֹ֣א חָמַ֗ל אֵ֚ת כָּל־נְא֣וֹת יַעֲקֹ֔ב הָרַ֧ס בְּעֶבְרָת֛וֹ מִבְצְרֵ֥י בַת־יְהוּדָ֖ה הִגִּ֣יעַ לָאָ֑רֶץ חִלֵּ֥ל מַמְלָכָ֖ה וְשָׂרֶֽיהָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has swallowed up [the] Lord, and not has he spared, all [the] pastures of Jacob; he has torn down in his fury [the] strongholds of [the] daughter of Judah; he has brought [them] to the ground; he has profaned [the] kingdom and its princes.

en.L: The Lord has swallowed up, and has not spared, all the dwellings of Jacob; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has torn down in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fury the strongholds of the daughter of Judah, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has brought [them] to the ground; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has profaned the kingdom and its princes.
en.B: The Lord has swallowed up without pity all the settlements of Jacob; \q in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fury {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has torn down the strongholds of Daughter Judah and brought them down to the ground; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has dishonored the kingdom and its officials.
en.R: The Lord swallowed up all the homes of Jacob's people and showed no pity. \q In {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fury {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} tore down the forts of the people of Judah and knocked them to the ground. \q He brought shame on the kingdom and its leaders.

decisions.choice: dwellings: the open settlements and pasture lands
decisions.reason: The word means pasture grounds and the homes of shepherds and farmers in open country. Set beside "strongholds", it covers the whole land: first the unwalled villages, then the fortified towns.

decisions.choice: has profaned: has stripped of its honor as something set apart
decisions.reason: The verb means to treat what is holy as common. The kingdom of David's line was set apart by God (Psalm 89:4-5); now God himself has thrown its honor to the ground (Psalm 89:40).

decisions.choice: daughter of Judah: the people of Judah pictured as a young woman
decisions.reason: As with "daughter of Zion" (verse 1), the land and its people are pictured as a daughter, one who could be loved, shamed and mourned.

decisions.choice: and has not spared
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "not" alone; the reading tradition adds "and". The sense is the same either way: he swallowed up without pity.

decisions.choice: officials (Balanced), leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word for the king's chief men (sar) is "princes" at Literal, as in Isaiah and Jeremiah; Balanced and Readable use "officials" and "leaders", since they were not the king's sons.

decisions.choice: Jacob's people ... the people of Judah
decisions.reason: Readable shows that Jacob and the daughter of Judah stand for the people.

source.text: גָּדַ֣ע בָּֽחֳרִיאַ֗ף כֹּ֚ל קֶ֣רֶן יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הֵשִׁ֥יב אָח֛וֹר יְמִינ֖וֹ מִפְּנֵ֣י אוֹיֵ֑ב וַיִּבְעַ֤ר בְּיַעֲקֹב֙ כְּאֵ֣שׁ לֶֽהָבָ֔ה אָכְלָ֖ה סָבִֽיב׃ס

records.literal_gloss: He has cut off in [the] heat of anger every horn of Israel; he has turned back backward his right hand from before [the] enemy; and he has burned in Jacob like a fire of flame [that] consumes all around.

en.L: He has cut off in burning anger every horn of Israel; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has drawn back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand from before the enemy, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has burned in Jacob like a flaming fire that consumes all around.
en.B: In blazing anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has cut down all the strength of Israel; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has pulled back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand in the face of the enemy; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has blazed through Jacob like a flaming fire that devours everything around it.
en.R: In {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} broke all of Israel's strength. \q He pulled back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand and did not protect them when the enemy attacked. \q He burned through the people of Jacob like a fire that destroys everything around it.

decisions.choice: horn: strength and power
decisions.reason: A horn is the strength of a wild ox, and so stands for power and pride (1 Samuel 2:1, 10; Psalm 75:11). Every horn cut off means all Israel's strength broken. The same picture returns in verse 17, where God raises the horn of Zion's enemies.

decisions.choice: his right hand: God's own hand, held back from helping
decisions.reason: God's right hand was the hand that fought for Israel (Exodus 15:6, 12). Now he draws it back when the enemy comes, and so Israel is left without defense. "His" could also be Israel's right hand, made useless in battle, but the Lord is the subject of every other verb in the verse.

decisions.choice: burned in Jacob: his anger spread through the people like fire
decisions.reason: Fire stands for God's anger, which spreads until nothing is left (Deuteronomy 32:22; Jeremiah 4:4).

decisions.choice: strength
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the horn stands for (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps the picture.

decisions.choice: did not protect them when the enemy attacked
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what the drawn-back hand meant for Israel (meaning decision m2).

source.text: דָּרַ֨ךְ קַשְׁתּ֜וֹ כְּאוֹיֵ֗ב נִצָּ֤ב יְמִינוֹ֙ כְּצָ֔ר וַֽיַּהֲרֹ֔ג כֹּ֖ל מַחֲמַדֵּי־עָ֑יִן בְּאֹ֨הֶל֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן שָׁפַ֥ךְ כָּאֵ֖שׁ חֲמָתֽוֹ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: He has bent his bow like an enemy, standing [with] his right hand like a foe, and he has killed all [the] delights of [the] eye; in [the] tent of [the] daughter of Zion he has poured out like fire his wrath.

en.L: He has bent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} bow like an enemy, with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand set like a foe, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has killed all that was precious to the eye; \q in the tent of the daughter of Zion {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has poured out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wrath like fire.
en.B: He has strung {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} bow like an enemy, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand poised like a foe; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has killed everyone who was a delight to see; \q on the tent of Daughter Zion {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has poured out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rage like fire.
en.R: He bent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} bow like an enemy. His right hand was ready to strike like a foe. \q He killed everyone we loved to look at. \q He poured out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger like fire on the homes of the people of Zion.

decisions.choice: bent his bow: strung it, ready to shoot
decisions.reason: The verb means "to tread": an archer pressed one end of a large bow down with his foot to string it (Psalm 7:13; Jeremiah 46:9).

decisions.choice: like an enemy: he acts as an enemy would
decisions.reason: The Lord is not said to have become Zion's enemy in name, but he does what an enemy does. The comparison returns in verse 5.

decisions.choice: all that was precious to the eye: the people Zion loved
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of a man's wife (Ezekiel 24:16) and of sons and daughters (Ezekiel 24:21, 25). Here it means the young men and children who were Zion's delight, though it may also include the temple's treasures (1:10).

decisions.choice: the tent of the daughter of Zion: her dwelling, the city itself
decisions.reason: "Tent" is an old word for home (Jeremiah 4:20; 10:20). It may point to the temple, but more likely to the city as Zion's home.

decisions.choice: the homes of the people of Zion
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the tent stands for (meaning decision m4).

source.text: הָיָ֨ה אֲדֹנָ֤י׀כְּאוֹיֵב֙ בִּלַּ֣ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בִּלַּע֙ כָּל־אַרְמְנוֹתֶ֔יהָ שִׁחֵ֖ת מִבְצָרָ֑יו וַיֶּ֨רֶב֙ בְּבַת־יְהוּדָ֔ה תַּאֲנִיָּ֖ה וַאֲנִיָּֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has become [the] Lord like an enemy; he has swallowed up Israel; he has swallowed up all its palaces; he has ruined its strongholds; and he has multiplied in [the] daughter of Judah mourning and moaning.

en.L: The Lord has become like an enemy; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has swallowed up Israel, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has swallowed up all its palaces, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has ruined its strongholds; \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has multiplied in the daughter of Judah mourning and moaning.
en.B: The Lord has become like an enemy: \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has swallowed up Israel, swallowed up all its palaces, and laid its strongholds in ruins; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has heaped up mourning and moaning in Daughter Judah.
en.R: The Lord acted like an enemy. \q He destroyed Israel completely. He wiped out all its palaces and ruined its forts. \q He made the people of Judah cry and grieve more and more.

decisions.choice: the Lord has become like an enemy
decisions.reason: The verse sums up verses 1-4. The God who fought for his people now fights against them, as the covenant warned he would (Leviticus 26:17, 24; Deuteronomy 28:63).

decisions.choice: its palaces ... its strongholds: the land and city of Israel
decisions.reason: The first "its" is feminine and the second masculine: the poet moves between Israel as a land or city and Israel as a people. Both mean the same place.

decisions.choice: mourning and moaning: two words from one root
decisions.reason: The two nouns sound alike and come from the same root, as in Isaiah 29:2. Grief is piled on grief.

decisions.choice: mourning and moaning
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced use two English words that sound alike, to echo the Hebrew pair (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: destroyed ... completely ... wiped out
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "swallowed up" means.

source.text: וַיַּחְמֹ֤ס כַּגַּן֙ שֻׂכּ֔וֹ שִׁחֵ֖ת מוֹעֲד֑וֹ שִׁכַּ֨ח יְהוָ֤ה׀בְּצִיּוֹן֙ מוֹעֵ֣ד וְשַׁבָּ֔ת וַיִּנְאַ֥ץ בְּזַֽעַם־אַפּ֖וֹ מֶ֥לֶךְ וְכֹהֵֽן׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And he has done violence like a garden [to] his booth; he has ruined his meeting place; has made forgotten YHWH in Zion appointed feast and sabbath; and he has spurned in [the] indignation of his anger king and priest.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done violence to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} booth as [to] a garden, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has ruined {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} meeting place; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has made appointed feast and Sabbath forgotten in Zion, \q and in the indignation of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has spurned king and priest.
en.B: He has torn down {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} booth as one strips a garden; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has ruined {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} place of meeting; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has wiped out the memory of festival and Sabbath in Zion, \q and in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has spurned both king and priest.
en.R: He tore down {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} temple as if it were only a shelter in a garden. He destroyed the place where people met with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} made the people of Zion forget the holy festivals and the Sabbath. \q In {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce anger {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rejected both the king and the priest.

decisions.choice: his booth: the temple, pulled down as easily as a garden shelter
decisions.reason: "Booth" is a shelter of branches. Here it is God's dwelling, the temple (compare Psalm 76:3, where his "shelter" is in Salem). "Like a garden" is brief and hard: it may mean he tore it down as one clears a garden, or as one pulls down a watchman's hut in a garden after the harvest (Isaiah 1:8). Either way, what seemed permanent was swept away.

decisions.choice: meeting place ... appointed feast: one word, two senses
decisions.reason: The same word (mo'ed) means first the place where God met his people and then the set times of worship held there. With the temple gone, the festivals and Sabbaths it served are gone too.

decisions.choice: king and priest: the two offices that led the nation
decisions.reason: Both the royal house and the priesthood are rejected. Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon, and the chief priests were executed (2 Kings 25:6-7, 18-21).

decisions.choice: his temple ... the place where people met with him
decisions.reason: Readable names what the booth and the meeting place stand for (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

source.text: זָנַ֨ח אֲדֹנָ֤י׀מִזְבְּחוֹ֙ נִאֵ֣ר מִקְדָּשׁ֔וֹ הִסְגִּיר֙ בְּיַד־אוֹיֵ֔ב חוֹמֹ֖ת אַרְמְנוֹתֶ֑יהָ ק֛וֹל נָתְנ֥וּ בְּבֵית־יְהוָ֖ה כְּי֥וֹם מוֹעֵֽד׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has rejected [the] Lord his altar; he has disowned his sanctuary; he has handed over into [the] hand of [the] enemy [the] walls of her palaces; a voice they gave in [the] house of YHWH as [on a] day of appointed feast.

en.L: The Lord has rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altar, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has disowned {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sanctuary; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has handed over into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; \q they raised [their] voice in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} as on a day of appointed feast.
en.B: The Lord has cast off {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altar and disowned {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sanctuary; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has handed the walls of her palaces over to the enemy; \q they raised a shout in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} as on a festival day.
en.R: The Lord rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own altar. He turned away from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy temple. \q He let the enemy take the walls of Jerusalem's palaces. \q The enemy shouted in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple, like people celebrating at a festival.

decisions.choice: disowned: rejected with disgust
decisions.reason: This verb is rare; in Psalm 89:40 it is used of God renouncing his covenant with David. Here he renounces his own sanctuary.

decisions.choice: they raised a shout: the enemy soldiers in the temple
decisions.reason: The subject is not named, but it is the enemy of the line before. Their shouts of victory filled the temple courts where Israel's festival songs used to sound (Psalm 74:4).

decisions.choice: her palaces: Zion's
decisions.reason: "Her" is Zion, the city, as through the chapter.

decisions.choice: Jerusalem's palaces ... The enemy shouted
decisions.reason: Readable names the city and the ones who shouted (meaning decisions m2 and m3).

source.text: חָשַׁ֨ב יְהוָ֤ה׀לְהַשְׁחִית֙ חוֹמַ֣ת בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן נָ֣טָה קָ֔ו לֹא־הֵשִׁ֥יב יָד֖וֹ מִבַּלֵּ֑עַ וַיַּֽאֲבֶל־חֵ֥ל וְחוֹמָ֖ה יַחְדָּ֥ו אֻמְלָֽלוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has planned YHWH to destroy [the] wall of [the] daughter of Zion; he has stretched out a line; not has he turned back his hand from swallowing up; and he has made mourn rampart and wall; together they have languished.

en.L: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stretched out a line, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not draw back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand from swallowing up; \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made rampart and wall mourn; together they have wasted away.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} resolved to tear down the wall of Daughter Zion; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stretched out the measuring line and did not hold back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand from destroying; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made rampart and wall lament; together they lie in ruins.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} decided to destroy the walls that protected the people of Zion. \q He measured them out for destruction and did not stop until {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had destroyed them. \q The walls and the defenses in front of them mourned, and they all crumbled together.

decisions.choice: stretched out a line: measured the city for destruction
decisions.reason: A builder's measuring line marked out what was to be built; here it marks out what is to be torn down, carefully and on purpose (2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11).

decisions.choice: rampart: the outer defensive wall or earthwork
decisions.reason: The word names the outer fortification in front of the main wall (2 Samuel 20:15; Isaiah 26:1).

decisions.choice: rampart and wall mourn: the ruined walls pictured as mourners
decisions.reason: The walls are pictured as people in grief (compare Isaiah 3:26; Jeremiah 14:2). The verb at the end means to waste away, to grow weak and faint.

decisions.choice: the walls that protected the people of Zion ... measured them out for destruction ... did not stop until he had destroyed them
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people of Zion" for "the daughter of Zion", as in verse 1. Readable explains the measuring line (meaning decision m1) and turns the negative "did not draw back his hand" into plain words.

source.text: טָבְע֤וּ בָאָ֨רֶץ֙ שְׁעָרֶ֔יהָ אִבַּ֥ד וְשִׁבַּ֖ר בְּרִיחֶ֑יהָ מַלְכָּ֨הּ וְשָׂרֶ֤יהָ בַגּוֹיִם֙ אֵ֣ין תּוֹרָ֔ה גַּם־נְבִיאֶ֕יהָ לֹא־מָצְא֥וּ חָז֖וֹן מֵיְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Have sunk into the ground her gates; he has destroyed and broken her bars; her king and her princes [are] among the nations; there is no instruction; also her prophets have not found a vision from YHWH.

en.L: Her gates have sunk into the ground; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has destroyed and broken her bars; \q her king and her princes [are] among the nations; there is no instruction; \q her prophets also have found no vision from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Her gates have sunk into the ground; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has wrecked and shattered her bars. \q Her king and her officials are among the nations; instruction is no more, \q and her prophets find no vision from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Jerusalem's gates have sunk into the ground. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} smashed the bars that locked them. \q Her king and her leaders now live among foreign nations. There is no more teaching from God. \q Her prophets do not receive any visions from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: bars: the beams that locked the city gates
decisions.reason: Heavy bars of wood or metal were set across the gates at night and in war (Deuteronomy 3:5; 1 Kings 4:13). With the bars broken and the gates buried in rubble, the city lay open.

decisions.choice: there is no instruction: God's teaching has ceased
decisions.reason: Instruction (torah) was the priests' task, as vision was the prophets' and counsel the elders' (Jeremiah 18:18; Ezekiel 7:26). With the temple gone and the leaders in exile, no one gives God's teaching. The words may also go with the line before: the king and officials are among nations where God's instruction is not known.

decisions.choice: no vision from the LORD: God is silent
decisions.reason: The prophets have nothing from God to say (Psalm 74:9; Ezekiel 7:26; compare 1 Samuel 3:1). Verse 14 says what their visions had been worth before the fall.

decisions.choice: officials (Balanced), leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2.

decisions.choice: Jerusalem's gates ... The LORD smashed ... teaching from God
decisions.reason: Readable names the city and the one who broke the bars, and says whose teaching has ceased (meaning decision m2). "Teaching" follows the wording used for torah in Isaiah.

source.text: יֵשְׁב֨וּ לָאָ֤רֶץ יִדְּמוּ֙ זִקְנֵ֣י בַת־צִיּ֔וֹן הֶֽעֱל֤וּ עָפָר֙ עַל־רֹאשָׁ֔ם חָגְר֖וּ שַׂקִּ֑ים הוֹרִ֤ידוּ לָאָ֨רֶץ֙ רֹאשָׁ֔ן בְּתוּלֹ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: They sit on the ground, they are silent, [the] elders of [the] daughter of Zion; they have thrown up dust on their head; they have girded on sackcloth; they have brought down to the ground their head, [the] virgins of Jerusalem.

en.L: The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground [and] are silent; \q they have thrown dust on their heads, they have put on sackcloth; \q the virgins of Jerusalem have bowed their heads to the ground.
en.B: The elders of Daughter Zion sit on the ground without a word; \q they have thrown dust on their heads and wrapped themselves in sackcloth; \q the young women of Jerusalem bow their heads low to the earth.
en.R: The elders of Zion sit silently on the ground. \q They throw dust on their heads and put on sackcloth to show their grief. \q The young women of Jerusalem hang their heads down to the ground.

decisions.choice: sitting on the ground, dust on the head, sackcloth: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: These were the usual acts of deep grief (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:8, 12-13; Jeremiah 6:26). Sackcloth was rough cloth of goat or camel hair worn by mourners. Silence too belonged to mourning (Job 2:13).

decisions.choice: virgins: young unmarried women
decisions.reason: The word names young women of marriageable age. Set beside the elders, the old men and the young women together stand for the whole population (1:4, 18).

decisions.choice: young women
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the age group the word refers to (meaning decision m2); Literal keeps "virgins".

decisions.choice: to show their grief
decisions.reason: Readable says why they put on sackcloth (meaning decision m1).

source.text: כָּל֨וּ בַדְּמָע֤וֹת עֵינַי֙ חֳמַרְמְר֣וּ מֵעַ֔י נִשְׁפַּ֤ךְ לָאָ֨רֶץ֙ כְּבֵדִ֔י עַל־שֶׁ֖בֶר בַּת־עַמִּ֑י בֵּֽעָטֵ֤ף עוֹלֵל֙ וְיוֹנֵ֔ק בִּרְחֹב֖וֹת קִרְיָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Are spent with tears my eyes; are in turmoil my inward parts; is poured out to the ground my liver over [the] breaking of [the] daughter of my people, as faint child and nursing [infant] in [the] squares of [the] town.

en.L: My eyes are spent with tears, my insides churn; \q my liver is poured out on the ground over the shattering of the daughter of my people, \q as child and nursing infant faint in the squares of the town.
en.B: My eyes are worn out with weeping, my stomach is in turmoil; \q my heart is poured out on the ground because my dear people are shattered, \q as little children and babies faint in the city squares.
en.R: My eyes are worn out from crying. I feel sick deep inside. \q I am overcome with grief because my people have been crushed. \q Little children and babies are fainting in the streets of the city.

decisions.choice: the poet speaks of himself
decisions.reason: After describing Zion's ruin (verses 1-10), the poet now speaks in the first person of his own grief. From verse 13 he will speak to Zion directly.

decisions.choice: my insides churn ... my liver is poured out: grief felt in the body
decisions.reason: The inner organs were thought of as the seat of feeling (1:20; Jeremiah 4:19). A liver poured out on the ground pictures a grief so deep the poet feels emptied of life.

decisions.choice: the daughter of my people: my people, loved like a daughter
decisions.reason: This phrase, common in Jeremiah (4:11; 8:21-23), pictures the people tenderly as a daughter. It is the poet's own people he weeps for.

decisions.choice: children fainting in the squares: the famine of the siege
decisions.reason: During Babylon's siege of Jerusalem the food ran out (2 Kings 25:3; Jeremiah 52:6). The squares were the open spaces inside the gates where people gathered.

decisions.choice: my heart (Balanced); my dear people (Balanced), my people (Readable)
decisions.reason: In English the heart, not the liver, is the seat of grief, so Balanced says "heart" and Readable "I am overcome with grief"; Literal keeps "liver". "The daughter of my people" is "my dear people" at Balanced and "my people" at Readable, as in Jeremiah.

source.text: לְאִמֹּתָם֙ יֹֽאמְר֔וּ אַיֵּ֖ה דָּגָ֣ן וָיָ֑יִן בְּהִֽתְעַטְּפָ֤ם כֶּֽחָלָל֙ בִּרְחֹב֣וֹת עִ֔יר בְּהִשְׁתַּפֵּ֣ךְ נַפְשָׁ֔ם אֶל־חֵ֖יק אִמֹּתָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: To their mothers they say, Where [is] grain and wine? as they faint like [the] wounded in [the] squares of [the] city, as is poured out their life into [the] bosom of their mothers.

en.L: To their mothers they say, "Where [are] grain and wine?" \q as they faint like the wounded in the squares of the city, \q as their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom.
en.B: They keep asking their mothers, "Where is there grain and wine?" \q as they collapse like the wounded in the city's open squares, \q while their life drains away in their mothers' arms.
en.R: They cry to their mothers, "Where is something to eat and drink?" \q They faint in the city streets like people wounded in battle. \q They die in their mothers' arms.

decisions.choice: grain and wine: the everyday food of the land
decisions.reason: Grain for bread and wine were the staples of daily life (Deuteronomy 7:13; Psalm 4:8). The children ask for what every household once had.

decisions.choice: the wounded: those struck down in battle
decisions.reason: The word means pierced or wounded, often fatally. The children collapse from hunger as soldiers fall from wounds.

decisions.choice: their life is poured out: they are dying
decisions.reason: Life poured out is life draining away (Psalm 22:15; Isaiah 53:12). The children die in their mothers' laps.

decisions.choice: they say: they keep asking
decisions.reason: The verb form describes something that goes on happening: the children ask again and again.

decisions.choice: something to eat and drink ... They die
decisions.reason: Readable says what grain and wine stand for (meaning decision m1) and says plainly what the idiom means (meaning decision m3).

source.text: מָֽה־אֲעִידֵ֞ךְ מָ֣ה אֲדַמֶּה־לָּ֗ךְ הַבַּת֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם מָ֤ה אַשְׁוֶה־לָּךְ֙ וַאֲנַֽחֲמֵ֔ךְ בְּתוּלַ֖ת בַּת־צִיּ֑וֹן כִּֽי־גָד֥וֹל כַּיָּ֛ם שִׁבְרֵ֖ךְ מִ֥י יִרְפָּא־לָֽךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: What shall I testify [for] you? What shall I liken to you, the daughter of Jerusalem? What shall I make equal to you, that I may comfort you, virgin daughter of Zion? For great like the sea [is] your breaking; who will heal you?

en.L: What can I testify for you? What can I liken to you, daughter of Jerusalem? \q What can I make equal to you, that I may comfort you, virgin daughter of Zion? \q For your breaking is great like the sea; who can heal you?
en.B: What witness can I bring for you? What can I liken to you, Daughter Jerusalem? \q What can I set beside you to comfort you, Virgin Daughter Zion? \q For the breach in you is as wide as the sea; who could heal you?
en.R: What can I say to you? What can I compare you with, people of Jerusalem? \q Is there anyone like you, so that I could comfort you, dear people of Zion? \q Your ruin is as huge as the sea. Who can make you well?

decisions.choice: the poet speaks to Zion
decisions.reason: Here the poet turns and speaks to Zion herself as "you". He goes on addressing her through verse 19.

decisions.choice: what can I testify for you: what example can I cite
alternatives: what can I say to you
what can I compare to you
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to bear witness. Here it probably means to bring forward a case like hers. Some read it, with small changes to the letters, as "what can I compare to you", which would match the next two questions.

decisions.choice: liken ... make equal ... comfort: a grief shared is a grief eased
decisions.reason: If the poet could find another city that had suffered so, Zion would not be alone in her pain (compare 1:12). He can find none.

decisions.choice: great like the sea: without limit
decisions.reason: The sea stands for what is vast and cannot be measured or crossed. Her "breaking" is the same word as in verse 11: her wound and her ruin.

decisions.choice: Virgin Daughter Zion (Balanced); dear people of Zion (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Virgin" pictures Zion as a young woman not yet married, cherished and protected (Isaiah 37:22). Readable says "dear people of Zion" to keep that tenderness. "The breach in you" at Balanced keeps the picture of a wound or broken wall.

source.text: נְבִיאַ֗יִךְ חָ֤זוּ לָךְ֙ שָׁ֣וְא וְתָפֵ֔ל וְלֹֽא־גִלּ֥וּ עַל־עֲוֺנֵ֖ךְ לְהָשִׁ֣יב שְׁבוּתֵ֑ךְ וַיֶּ֣חֱזוּ לָ֔ךְ מַשְׂא֥וֹת שָׁ֖וְא וּמַדּוּחִֽים׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Your prophets have seen for you emptiness and whitewash, and not have they uncovered your iniquity to restore your fortunes; and they have seen for you oracles of emptiness and enticements.

en.L: Your prophets have seen for you emptiness and whitewash, \q and they have not exposed your iniquity, to restore your fortunes; \q they have seen for you oracles of emptiness and enticements.
en.B: The visions your prophets saw for you were empty and worthless; \q they did not lay bare your guilt to turn back your captivity; \q the oracles they saw for you were hollow and misleading.
en.R: Your prophets told you about visions that were worthless lies. \q They did not point out your sin. If they had, you might not have been taken away as captives. \q The messages they gave you were empty and led you the wrong way.

decisions.choice: emptiness and whitewash: worthless, covering up the cracks
decisions.reason: "Emptiness" is what has no truth or substance. The second word is used by Ezekiel for whitewash smeared over a weak wall to hide its cracks (Ezekiel 13:10-15; 22:28): these prophets covered over the people's sin. It can also mean tasteless and insipid (Job 6:6).

decisions.choice: to restore your fortunes: to turn back what was coming
decisions.reason: The phrase means to bring about a reversal, often a return from captivity (Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3). If the prophets had exposed the people's sin, they might have turned back to God and been spared exile. The written Hebrew text and the reading tradition spell the noun slightly differently; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: oracles of emptiness and enticements: false messages that led astray
decisions.reason: "Oracles" is the word for a prophet's message from God (Isaiah 13:1). The last word is found only here; it comes from a root meaning "to drive away", and may mean messages that misled the people or that led to their being driven into exile (Jeremiah 27:10, 15).

decisions.choice: your prophets: those who promised peace
decisions.reason: Jeremiah faced prophets who said "Peace, peace" when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14; 14:13-16; 23:16-17; 28).

decisions.choice: guilt (Balanced), sin (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word for iniquity is "guilt" at Balanced and "sin" at Readable, as in Isaiah.

decisions.choice: If they had, you might not have been taken away as captives
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the purpose clause as a consequence (meaning decision m2).

source.text: סָֽפְק֨וּ עָלַ֤יִךְ כַּפַּ֨יִם֙ כָּל־עֹ֣בְרֵי דֶ֔רֶךְ שָֽׁרְקוּ֙ וַיָּנִ֣עוּ רֹאשָׁ֔ם עַל־בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם הֲזֹ֣את הָעִ֗יר שֶׁיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ כְּלִ֣ילַת יֹ֔פִי מָשׂ֖וֹשׂ לְכָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Have clapped at you hands all passers of [the] way; they have hissed and shaken their head at [the] daughter of Jerusalem: Is this the city that they called, Perfect of beauty, a joy to all the earth?

en.L: All who pass along the way have clapped [their] hands at you; \q they have hissed and shaken their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem: \q "Is this the city of which they said, 'Perfect in beauty, a joy to all the earth'?"
en.B: All who travel the road clap their hands at you; \q they hiss in scorn and shake their heads at Daughter Jerusalem: \q "Is this the city people called 'perfect in beauty, the delight of the whole earth'?"
en.R: Everyone who walks by claps their hands at you. \q They make mocking sounds and shake their heads at the people of Jerusalem. They say, \q "Is this the city that people called the most beautiful city, the joy of the whole world?"

decisions.choice: clapping, hissing, shaking the head: gestures of scorn and horror
decisions.reason: Passers-by react to a ruined place with these gestures (1 Kings 9:8; Jeremiah 18:16; 19:8; Psalm 22:8; Job 27:23). They mock and are appalled at once.

decisions.choice: perfect in beauty, a joy to all the earth: Zion's old praises
decisions.reason: Psalm 50:2 calls Zion "the perfection of beauty", and Psalm 48:3 calls it "the joy of all the earth". The passers-by throw those words back at the ruined city.

decisions.choice: the passers-by speak
decisions.reason: The question is what the travelers say. The words they quote are what people used to say about Zion.

decisions.choice: hissed (Literal), hiss in scorn (Balanced), make mocking sounds (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb is the hiss or whistle of scorn that Jeremiah's lists call a "hissing" (Jeremiah 19:8). Balanced and Readable say what the sound meant, as the wording for that list does.

decisions.choice: They say
decisions.reason: Readable introduces the question as speech.

source.text: פָּצ֨וּ עָלַ֤יִךְ פִּיהֶם֙ כָּל־א֣וֹיְבַ֔יִךְ שָֽׁרְקוּ֙ וַיַּֽחַרְקוּ־שֵׁ֔ן אָמְר֖וּ בִּלָּ֑עְנוּ אַ֣ךְ זֶ֥ה הַיּ֛וֹם שֶׁקִּוִּינֻ֖הוּ מָצָ֥אנוּ רָאִֽינוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Have opened against you their mouth all your enemies; they have hissed and gnashed tooth; they have said, We have swallowed [her] up! Surely this [is] the day that we have hoped for it; we have found, we have seen!

en.L: All your enemies have opened their mouths against you; \q they have hissed and gnashed [their] teeth; they have said, "We have swallowed [her] up! \q Surely this is the day that we hoped for; we have found [it], we have seen [it]!"
en.B: All your enemies open their mouths wide against you; \q they hiss and grind their teeth and say, "We have swallowed her up! \q It has come at last, the day we hoped for; we have found it, we have seen it with our own eyes!"
en.R: All your enemies open their mouths wide to make fun of you. \q They hiss and grind their teeth and say, "We have destroyed her! \q This is the day we have been waiting for. Now it has come, and we have seen it!"

decisions.choice: pe before ayin
decisions.reason: This verse begins with pe and the next with ayin, the reverse of chapter 1's order; see verse 1.

decisions.choice: open mouths and gnashing teeth: hatred and gloating
decisions.reason: To open the mouth wide against someone is to jeer at them (Psalm 35:21; Isaiah 57:4); grinding the teeth shows hatred (Psalm 35:16; 37:12). Like the passers-by of verse 15, the enemies hiss.

decisions.choice: we have found, we have seen: our hope has come true
decisions.reason: The two short verbs stand side by side without "and": the enemies have reached the day they hoped for and see it with their own eyes. The word "swallowed up" is the same verb the poet used of the Lord (verses 2, 5); the enemies boast of what was God's doing (verse 17).

decisions.choice: [her] ... [it]
decisions.reason: The Hebrew verbs have no object; Literal supplies them in brackets and Balanced supplies them plainly.

decisions.choice: to make fun of you ... destroyed
decisions.reason: Readable says what the open mouths mean (meaning decision m2) and what "swallowed up" means.

source.text: עָשָׂ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר זָמָ֗ם בִּצַּ֤ע אֶמְרָתוֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוָּ֣ה מִֽימֵי־קֶ֔דֶם הָרַ֖ס וְלֹ֣א חָמָ֑ל וַיְשַׂמַּ֤ח עָלַ֨יִךְ֙ אוֹיֵ֔ב הֵרִ֖ים קֶ֥רֶן צָרָֽיִךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has done YHWH what he planned; he has carried out his word which he commanded from days of old; he has torn down and not has he spared; and he has made rejoice over you [the] enemy; he has raised [the] horn of your foes.

en.L: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has done what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} planned; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has carried out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} commanded from days of old; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has torn down and has not spared; \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made the enemy rejoice over you, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has raised high the horn of your foes.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has done what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} purposed; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has fulfilled {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word, which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} decreed long ago; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has thrown down without pity; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has let the enemy gloat over you and raised up the strength of your foes.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} did what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had planned. He did what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had warned long ago that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would do. \q He tore you down and showed no pity. \q He let your enemies celebrate over you. He made your enemies strong.

decisions.choice: his word that he commanded from days of old: the warnings of the covenant
decisions.reason: Long before, the covenant had warned what would happen if Israel turned from the LORD: siege, famine, exile and ruin (Leviticus 26:14-39; Deuteronomy 28:15-68). The fall of Jerusalem is that word carried out.

decisions.choice: the LORD has done what he planned: the enemy's boast answered
decisions.reason: The enemies claimed the victory as theirs (verse 16); the poet says it was the LORD's plan (compare Jeremiah 4:28; 51:12). The verse begins with ayin, after the pe of verse 16 (see verse 1).

decisions.choice: raised the horn of your foes: made them strong and proud
decisions.reason: The horn stands for strength, as in verse 3. The LORD cut off Israel's horn and raised the enemy's.

decisions.choice: strength (Balanced); made your enemies strong (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 3, Balanced and Readable say what the horn stands for.

decisions.choice: what he had warned long ago that he would do
decisions.reason: Readable says what "his word which he commanded" was (meaning decision m1).

source.text: צָעַ֥ק לִבָּ֖ם אֶל־אֲדֹנָ֑י חוֹמַ֣ת בַּת־צִ֠יּוֹן הוֹרִ֨ידִי כַנַּ֤חַל דִּמְעָה֙ יוֹמָ֣ם וָלַ֔יְלָה אַֽל־תִּתְּנִ֤י פוּגַת֙ לָ֔ךְ אַל־תִּדֹּ֖ם בַּת־עֵינֵֽךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Has cried out their heart to [the] Lord. Wall of [the] daughter of Zion, cause to run down like a torrent tear[s] day and night; do not give rest to yourself; let not be still [the] daughter of your eye.

en.L: Their heart cried out to the Lord. \q Wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a torrent day and night; \q do not give yourself relief; do not let the daughter of your eye be still.
en.B: Their heart cries out to the Lord. \q Wall of Daughter Zion, pour down tears like a torrent by day and by night! \q Give yourself no relief; do not let your eyes rest.
en.R: The people cry out to the Lord from their hearts. \q You walls of Zion, let your tears flow like a flood all day and all night! \q Do not stop to rest. Do not let your eyes stop crying.

decisions.choice: their heart cried out: the people's cry to the Lord
alternatives: Cry out from your heart to the Lord
decisions.reason: "Their" has no clear subject; it most likely means the people of Zion. The line is hard, and with a small change to the letters some read it as a command that goes with what follows: "Cry out from your heart to the Lord, wall of Daughter Zion".

decisions.choice: wall of the daughter of Zion: the city wall called to weep
decisions.reason: The poet calls on the wall, which mourned in verse 8, to stand for the whole city and weep without end (compare Jeremiah 9:17; 14:17).

decisions.choice: the daughter of your eye: the pupil, the eye itself
decisions.reason: This is a Hebrew name for the pupil of the eye (compare Psalm 17:8). Do not let it rest means: keep weeping.

decisions.choice: your eyes
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the daughter of your eye" means (meaning decision m3); Literal keeps the picture.

decisions.choice: The people cry out ... from their hearts
decisions.reason: Readable names who cries out, following meaning decision m1.

source.text: ק֣וּמִי׀רֹ֣נִּי בַלַּ֗יְלָה לְרֹאשׁ֙ אַשְׁמֻר֔וֹת שִׁפְכִ֤י כַמַּ֨יִם֙ לִבֵּ֔ךְ נֹ֖כַח פְּנֵ֣י אֲדֹנָ֑י שְׂאִ֧י אֵלָ֣יו כַּפַּ֗יִךְ עַל־נֶ֨פֶשׁ֙ עֽוֹלָלַ֔יִךְ הָעֲטוּפִ֥ים בְּרָעָ֖ב בְּרֹ֥אשׁ כָּל־חוּצֽוֹת׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Arise, cry out in the night, at [the] beginning of [the] watches; pour out like water your heart in front of [the] face of [the] Lord; lift up to him your palms for [the] life of your children, the ones fainting from hunger at [the] head of all streets.

en.L: Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches; \q pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord; \q lift up your palms to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for the life of your children, \q who faint from hunger at the head of every street.
en.B: Get up and cry aloud in the night, as each watch of the night begins; \q empty out your heart like water before the Lord's face. \q Raise your hands to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for the lives of your little ones, \q who grow faint from hunger at the corner of every street.
en.R: Get up and cry out in the night, again and again all through the night. \q Pour out all your feelings to the Lord like water. \q Lift up your hands to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in prayer, and beg {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to save the lives of your children. \q They are fainting from hunger on every street corner.

decisions.choice: at the beginning of the watches: all through the night
decisions.reason: The night was divided into watches (Judges 7:19; Psalm 63:7). To cry out as each one begins is to keep praying the whole night.

decisions.choice: pour out your heart like water: tell God all your grief
decisions.reason: To pour out the heart or soul is to hold nothing back in prayer (1 Samuel 1:15; Psalm 62:9; 142:3).

decisions.choice: lift up your palms: the posture of prayer
decisions.reason: People prayed with open hands raised toward God (Exodus 9:29; Psalm 28:2; 1 Kings 8:22).

decisions.choice: in the night
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text and the reading tradition spell the word for night differently; the sense is the same. This verse has four lines, the only one in the chapter with more than three.

decisions.choice: again and again ... in prayer ... beg him to save
decisions.reason: Readable explains the night watches and the lifted hands (meaning decisions m1 and m3).

source.text: רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וְֽהַבִּ֔יטָה לְמִ֖י עוֹלַ֣לְתָּ כֹּ֑ה אִם־תֹּאכַ֨לְנָה נָשִׁ֤ים פִּרְיָם֙ עֹלֲלֵ֣י טִפֻּחִ֔ים אִם־יֵהָרֵ֛ג בְּמִקְדַּ֥שׁ אֲדֹנָ֖י כֹּהֵ֥ן וְנָבִֽיא׃ס

records.literal_gloss: See, YHWH, and look: to whom have you dealt thus? Shall eat women their fruit, children of [their] tender care? Shall be killed in [the] sanctuary of [the] Lord priest and prophet?

en.L: See, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and look: to whom have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} done this? \q Should women eat their fruit, the children they have tended? \q Should priest and prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?
en.B: Look, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and take note: whom have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} ever dealt with like this? \q Must women eat their own offspring, the little ones they cared for? \q Must priest and prophet be slain in the Lord's sanctuary?
en.R: Zion cries: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, look and see! Have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} ever done this to anyone else? \q Should mothers eat their own children, the babies they took care of? \q Should priests and prophets be killed in the Lord's temple?

decisions.choice: Zion now speaks to the LORD
decisions.reason: The poet urged Zion to pray (verses 18-19); here she does. Zion's own voice speaks to the LORD from here to the end of the chapter (verse 22), as she did in 1:11-22.

decisions.choice: women eating their children: the worst curse of the covenant
decisions.reason: The covenant warned that in a siege people would eat their own children (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57). It happened in the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29) and here in Jerusalem (4:10).

decisions.choice: children they have tended: little ones carried and cared for
decisions.reason: The phrase means children nursed and carried in the arms. Hebrew "dealt" ('olalta) and "children" ('olele) sound alike: "to whom have you done this" points to the children.

decisions.choice: should ...? should ...?: questions of horror
decisions.reason: The two questions expect the answer "no": these things must never happen. Yet they have.

decisions.choice: mothers ... their own children ... the Lord's temple
decisions.reason: Readable says "mothers", since the women are eating their own children, and "temple" for the sanctuary.

decisions.choice: Zion cries:
decisions.reason: Readable marks the change of speaker, as in 1:9, 11 and 18 (m1).

source.text: שָׁכְב֨וּ לָאָ֤רֶץ חוּצוֹת֙ נַ֣עַר וְזָקֵ֔ן בְּתוּלֹתַ֥י וּבַחוּרַ֖י נָפְל֣וּ בֶחָ֑רֶב הָרַ֨גְתָּ֙ בְּי֣וֹם אַפֶּ֔ךָ טָבַ֖חְתָּ לֹ֥א חָמָֽלְתָּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: They have lain on the ground [in the] streets, young and old; my virgins and my young men have fallen by [the] sword; you have killed [them] in [the] day of your anger; you have slaughtered, not have you spared.

en.L: Young and old lie on the ground in the streets; \q my virgins and my young men have fallen by the sword; \q {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have killed [them] in the day of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} anger, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have slaughtered [them], {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have not spared.
en.B: Young and old lie on the ground in the streets; \q my young women and my young men have fallen by the sword. \q In the day of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} anger {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} struck them down; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} butchered them and did not spare.
en.R: Young people and old people lie dead on the ground in the streets. \q My young women and young men were killed by the sword. \q You killed them when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} were angry. You slaughtered them and showed no mercy.

decisions.choice: young and old: everyone
decisions.reason: The pair names the two ends of life and so everyone between. The young women and young men of the next line are the city's hope for the future.

decisions.choice: you have killed: Zion lays the deaths before God
decisions.reason: The enemy's sword did the killing, but Zion speaks to the LORD as the one behind it (verses 1-8, 17). She does not deny her sin (1:18), but she cries out at what his anger has done.

decisions.choice: slaughtered: killed like animals for meat
decisions.reason: The verb is used of butchering animals (Genesis 43:16). It is a shocking word for the death of the young.

decisions.choice: young women
decisions.reason: As in verse 10.

decisions.choice: lie dead
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that those lying in the streets are dead, as the next lines say.

source.text: תִּקְרָא֩ כְי֨וֹם מוֹעֵ֤ד מְגוּרַי֙ מִסָּבִ֔יב וְלֹ֥א הָיָ֛ה בְּי֥וֹם אַף־יְהוָ֖ה פָּלִ֣יט וְשָׂרִ֑יד אֲשֶׁר־טִפַּ֥חְתִּי וְרִבִּ֖יתִי אֹיְבִ֥י כִלָּֽם׃פ

records.literal_gloss: You summoned as [on a] day of appointed feast my terrors from all around; and there was not in [the] day of [the] anger of YHWH an escapee or a survivor; those whom I cared for and reared my enemy has finished them.

en.L: You summoned, as for a day of appointed feast, my terrors from all around, \q and in the day of the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there was no one who escaped or survived; \q those whom I nursed and raised, my enemy has destroyed them.
en.B: As if calling a festival crowd, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} summoned terrors against me from every side; \q on the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s anger no one escaped and no one survived; \q the children I nursed and brought up, my enemy has wiped out.
en.R: You called terrors to attack me from every side, the way people are called to a festival. \q On the day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was angry, no one escaped or survived. \q My enemy destroyed the children I cared for and raised.

decisions.choice: as for a day of appointed feast: a bitter festival
decisions.reason: Once Jerusalem was summoned to the LORD's feasts (verses 6-7); now he has summoned terrors to it, as if to a festival. The same picture is in 1:15.

decisions.choice: my terrors from all around: Jeremiah's "terror on every side"
decisions.reason: The words echo a phrase Jeremiah used again and again (Jeremiah 6:25; 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29; also Psalm 31:14).

decisions.choice: whom I nursed and raised: the children Zion brought up
decisions.reason: The first verb is the one behind "tended" in verse 20; Zion speaks as a mother of the children she cared for.

decisions.choice: my enemy: the chapter ends on the enemy
decisions.reason: Zion's prayer ends without an answer, with the enemy who has made an end of her children. Chapter 1 also closes with Zion's prayer about her enemies (1:21-22).

decisions.choice: terrors
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the plural "terrors" for the dangers that came from every side.
